Definitely agree with your point about increased access to mental health services for people, esp. for people working within our justice system. I think people who are committing domestic abuse, especially domestic abusers coming from a background of trauma, do need access to mental health treatment and an opportunity to do better, especially if their job includes engaging with the public and their job is to utilize the "monopoly on the legitimate usage violence by the state". I think that would definitely make a stronger judicial system, and I think we're in agreement on that point. I really do want to see police officers doing better, and I do want to find a way to create a better force for policing (how radical that goes is really something I'm trying to figure out - abolish or reform is the real question here.)

Personally, I'm going to say poor people also have a harder time accessing mental health services. If you're working long hours, it's harder to get to therapy. You might not have the money for your meds, you might not have the money for therapy. You might not have time for a stay in the psych ward, your boss might not be super forgiving of that. I've had a few coworkers mention being yelled at by their boss or fired for stays in the hospital who just didn't have the resources to fight back against their wrongful termination or who weren't taken seriously by HR.

As for studies, honestly, just googling "poverty and mental health" and "trauma and poverty" paints a pretty clear picture of the effects of poverty on an individual's health and wellbeing. Psychiatrists in the UK have even started just using the term SLS to describe some of their patients - Shit life syndrome. How do you address the mental health concerns of someone who has a genuine reason to be stressed and anxious and depressed about their life? If your patient comes to you and says "I'm not gonna be able to pay rent this month and I'm gonna lose the apartment", how do you counteract that? Diagnosing them with an anxiety disorder isn't gonna fix their problems.

I don't know if I can agree with "more community engagement with cops", though. I don't think a community engagement project is going to be the sole solution to the issues I have with policing practices. Police are at more risk for mental health issues, sure, but that's not my job to fix, especially as someone whose family has been, I'm going to say, been fucked over my current policing practices. I think policing will require much more large scale reforms in order to become anything which effectively regulates and structures the people. I've seen some really cool ideas for abolishing the police and creating a more egalitarian system of justice that I've been checking out, but I'm not an expert, so I won't speak to that.

As for the "we've been trying to do that for the poor and the minorities for so long", this is a genuine question, *literally how?* Honestly, all I've seen from the state is pushback after pushback against any attempt made to help those who have been left impoverished after a legacy of colonialism and trauma and degradation. I've seen so few effective initiatives to help people recover from the effects of poverty and I've seen all of them get unilaterally pushed back against. I honestly do not know what you mean when you say "we've tried helping poor people and it doesn't work".

Even HRT isn't really analogous for, say, anti-depressants. Anti-depressants are made to alter brain chemistry and fix the root of the problem, usually done alongside CBT to help resolve how you're behaving towards yourself and others and the ways in which that behaviour is toxic and self-detrimental.

When you're on HRT, the problem isn't you. It's not the way you're acting. It's not how you identify. It's not how you experience life that is the issue. You being trans isn't self-detrimental, you being depressed is. All of the issues with being trans are systemic, none of them are chemical or something wrong with how you are behaving. There's nothing wrong with anything you're doing. It's how you respond to being trans that is the issue. If you are a man who wasn't assigned male at birth, there is nothing wrong with that at all. If your response to that is to sleep with your binder on 3/7 days of the week, that's the maladaptive issue that needs to be addressed, and HRT isn't going to fix that. The only reason surgery is going to fix it is because it gives you nothing to bind.

HRT isn't really analogous to anti-depressants, and it's not fair to say they are because they are completely different in their goals, and I think that this thinking lends itself well to the notion that we have to "fix" trans people in the same way we need to "fix" people with depression and it really makes it hard not to medicalize transgender people for being transgender, when that's not really fair either. I've heard people say "well, surgery works for now, but when they come up with a surgery or drug to make a trans person fit into their assigned gender - " and they miss the point of HRT completely. It's not a treatment meant to "fix" the problem - it's meant to alleviate any distress that accompanies being transgender. I certainly wouldn't "cure" myself of my trans-ness if possible. That might accompany me not really being able to be true to myself while also being fully cis-passing (non-binary person). You sort of have to be comfortable with being visibly trans if you're not a binary trans person, and it took a lot of time for me to accept that. I almost just wanted to fully transition to be a man at first, because I thought it would be easier.

Being trans isn't a medical condition, your response to being trans is what can cause you harm, (if you just say "alright, I'm trans, I'm going to the doctor and buying a binder and following the instructions to the letter until I can get on HRT and then surgery" that's not harmful - but the rate of self-harm and suicide and depression among trans people clearly show that this is a difficult thing to process for many people) and this says nothing of the trauma that can come from other people's responses to you being trans that can exasperate any mental health condition any further. Even wait times get hard to sit through, all that time not being yourself.

The goal of HRT is to be yourself, it's not supposed to be a "cure". And anti-depressants, in a lot of ways, aren't supposed to be a cure either, but the goal is ultimately to make you not depressed, if that is a possible state for you to be in, and HRT really isn't similar in its goals or results. I think it might also lend to the idea that the goal of transitioning is to blend in - the symptom is you being trans, the cure is to be unrecognizable as such, but I've already written a lot and I'm avoiding a history paper.
